> Given that PLA-depleted strains are less likely than wild-type strains to kill their rat hosts, and may take longer to kill them,
one might think that selection for PLA depletion
could be driven by a classical transmission-virulence tradeoff
[@Lens1988; @LensMay1994; @Cres+2016].  However, the standard tradeoff
theory assumes that a longer generation interval will
correspond to more opportunities to transmit, and thus a greater basic reproduction number
($\rzero$). Because plague is transmitted from one rat host to
another primarily when the initial host dies and its fleas seek a new
host [@KeelGill2000], the infectious period is typically only a brief
moment at the end of the initial host's life. Thus, increasing
host survival time only increases the generation time between successsive infections
without allowing for more transmission, slowing the epidemic without affecting
$\rzero$.  Moreover, since PLA-depleted strains have lower
fatality proportions, they will actually cause fewer secondary infections
and hence have lower $\rzero$.

> We suggest two other mechanisms that may instead be responsible for inducing selection for PLA depletion after the wild type is established.  First, while less virulent and less transmissible strains are handicapped in competing with the wild type strain in the early phase of the epidemic, as the rat population is reduced in size, these "weaker" strains will be less likely to go extinct during epidemic troughs.  Second, rats infected with strains that kill more slowly will be more likely to disperse while infected, enhancing pathogen persistence through colonization of uninfected areas. These mechanisms are discussed further in SOM.

> plague is primarily transmitted from one host to another during a very short
> late-stage high bacteremia, which leads to the death of the initial host and movement

> reductions in the size and density of peridomestic rat populations during repeated

We were inspired by @Pars+2024, which suggests that lowering within-population $\rzero$ (from $\approx 2$) could decrease the probability of burnout in the trough after the initial introduction of plague into

* **demographic models matter**: @Pars+2024 considered only the case where hosts are replenished at a constant rate (i.e., absolute birth rate), which is reasonable for a disease with low impact on population size. For rat populations affected by plague, however, a logistic growth model (birth rate/susceptible replenishment rate proportional to population size) is more reasonable. (Also mention different $\epsilon$ value
* **simple metapopulation models may not work**: in stochastic simulation models of plague in rat metapopulations, we find a 'ratchet' effect: because persistence is extremely likely once an epidemic survives through the first trough, and since (enhancement via population suppression)
* starting on seasonality

## open questions/questioning assumptions

* is the enhanced possibility of colonization (through increased survival)
* should we be considering possibilities other than the classic rat-flea transmission cycle? (evolution in humans, e.g. importance of human ectoparasite/pneumonic transmission modes?)
* are there any other ways that historical or ancient-DNA evidence can shed light on the ancient ecology of plague? e.g.
   * evidence of host (rat) coevolution with plague
   * finding out more about the sylvatic cycle
   * proxies for historical rat populations
   
General point that ancient DNA can tell us an astonishing amount about organism-level biology, but ecology is harder (although not impossible; coalescents etc.)
